title: Kerria japonica

{{Short description|Species of shrub}} {{Speciesbox | image = Kerria japonica01.jpg|Natural form Kerria japonica - flower.jpg|Cultivar 'Pleniflora' Wild Kerria japonica with semi-double flowers in Fukushima (B).jpg|Wild semi-double form in Fukushima | image_caption = | display_parents = 3 | genus = Kerria (plant) | parent_authority = [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle|DC.]] | species = japonica | authority = ([[Carl Linnaeus|L.]]) [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle|DC.]] }} [[File:Afbeelding-063-Kerria japonica.tif|thumb|''Kerria japonica'' by [[Abraham Jacobus Wendel]], 1868]] '''''Kerria japonica''''', commonly known as '''Japanese kerria'''{{Cite web|title=''Kerria japonica''|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/kerria-japonica/|access-date=16 March 2021|website=North Carolina Extension: Gardener Plant Toolbox}} or '''Japanese rose''',{{Cite web|title=''Kerria japonica''|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=KEJA|access-date=16 March 2021|website=USDA Plants Database}} is a [[deciduous]], yellow-flowering [[shrub]] in the rose [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] ([[Rosaceae]]), [[native plant|native]] to China and Japan. It is the only species in the genus '''''Kerria'''''. In the wild, it grows in thickets on mountain slopes. Japanese kerria has been used for medicine and is also planted in gardens. A double-flowered [[cultivar]], ''K. japonica'' 'Pleniflora', is commonly called '''bachelor's buttons'''. When cultivated in the Central-Southern U.S., the plant is usually called '''Yellow Rose of Texas'''. Although the genus Kerria is in the rose family, it is not a true rose. ==Name== The genus name ''Kerria'' is also a common name for the species ('''Kerria'''). It is named after Scottish gardener [[William Kerr (gardener)|William Kerr]], who introduced the Japanese kerria [[cultivar]] 'Pleniflora'. In addition to the common names mentioned above, it is also known as '''Japanese marigold bush''' or '''miracle marigold bush''' in northern [[New England]],{{citation needed|date=March 2021}} although ''K. japonica'' is not closely related to the true marigolds (''[[Calendula]]'' spp.), which are [[asterids]]. It is sometimes known by its Japanese name ''yamabuki'' ({{lang|ja|山吹/ヤマブキ}}){{cite dictionary |author=Cannon, Garland Hampton |year=1996|encyclopedia=The Japanese contributions to the English language: an historical dictionary|title=yamabuki|location=Wiesbaden|publisher=Harrassowitz Verlag|page=136|isbn=3-447-03764-4}} lit. "mountain [[Petasites|butterbur]]" or "mountain breeze"); its Chinese name is ''dìtáng (huā)'' ({{lang|zh|棣棠[花]}}).{{eFloras | 2 | 200010868 | ''Kerria japonica'' | nv | access-date = 10 December 2023 }} ==Description== ''Kerria japonica'' grows to {{cvt|1-3|m|ft|0}} tall, with weak arching stems often scrambling over other vegetation or rocks. In the wild it grows in thickets on mountain slopes. The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, simple, {{cvt|3–10|cm|0}} long, with a doubly serrated margin. The [[flower]]s are golden yellow, with five [[petals]], and evenly-spaced along branches of new green growth. The [[fruit]] is a dry single-[[seed]]ed [[achene]] {{cvt|4–4.5|mm|2}} long.{{cite web|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200010868 |title=''Kerria japonica'' |author=Li Chao-luang, Hiroshi Ikeda |author2= Hideaki Ohba |work=Flora of China |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA |accessdate=8 July 2012}} ==Cultivation== Kerria is valued in gardens for its golden yellow flowers, which appear in the spring. It is best grown with some shade from full sunlight to avoid blanching the flowers, and needs to be pruned after flowering to maintain health and vigour.{{cite web | url = http://homeguides.sfgate.com/prune-kerria-japonica-20445.html | title = How to prune a ''Kerria japonica'' | publisher = SF Gate Homeguides | accessdate = 17 March 2018}} Two [[cultivars]] have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]], ''K. japonica'' 'Golden guinea'{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Kerria japonica'' 'Golden Guinea'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/47031/Kerria-japonica-Golden-Guinea/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|accessdate=27 September 2020}} and the double-flowered ''K. japonica'' 'Pleniflora', commonly known as bachelor's buttons.{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Kerria japonica'' 'Pleniflora'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/97763/Kerria-japonica-Pleniflora-(d)/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|accessdate=27 September 2020}}{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 57 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 14 March 2018}} ==Pests and diseases== Since 2014 the UK's Royal Horticultural Society has been receiving reports from gardeners and horticulturalists of damage to plants of the shrub ''Kerria japonica''. Symptoms include multiple red spots on leaves, and [[lesion]]s on the stems, resulting in [[defoliation]] and eventual death. It has been determined that this infection is caused by the fungus ''[[Blumeriella kerriae]]'', which is specific to the kerria. This highly contagious disease, known in English as kerria twig and leaf blight, was known in the U.S. but has not previously been observed on British plants. It is regarded as a serious threat to the cultivated kerria plants, which are popular garden shrubs.{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/advice/profile?pid=1018 | title = Kerria twig and leaf blight | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 16 March 2018}} ==Medicinal use== The plant has [[anti-inflammatory]] properties and a [[decoction]] of the flowering shoots with [[honey]] has been used in China in the treatment of [[cough]]s and [[Gynaecology|gynecological disorders]].{{cite dictionary|author=Quattrocchi, Umberto |year=2012|title=''Kerria japonica''|encyclopedia=CRC World dictionary of medicinal and poisonous plants: common names, scientific names, eponyms, synonyms and etymology|publisher=CRC Press Taylor and Francis Group|volume= III E-L|pages=661-2}}{{cite book|author=Duke, A. |author2= Ayensu, Edward S.|title=Medicinal Plants of China|publisher=Reference Publications, inc.|year=1985|volume= II |isbn=0-917256-27-1 |page=546}} ==Chemistry== The leaves and roots contain 0.002% [[hydrogen cyanide]], while the tender shoots are a rich source of [[vitamin C]] (200 mg per 100 g) and the seeds contain 44.9% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]] and 45.3% [[vegetable oil|fat]]. The flower petals contain the [[O-methylated flavonoid|''O''-methylated flavonoid]] [[pectolinarin]], (5,7-dihydroxy-4,6-dimethoxyflavone-7-rutinoside), a [[Cytotoxicity|cytotoxic]] compound known also as Neolinarin and found also in ''[[Linaria]]'' species, ''[[Kickxia elatine]]'' and the ''[[Duranta]]'' species ''D. plumieri''.{{cite book|author=Blunt, John W. |author2=Munro, Murray H. |} ''Kerria japonica'' is mentioned frequently in the ''[[Man'yōshū]]'', the oldest extant collection of Japanese poetry from the AD first millennium. In addition, the Japanese call the golden yellow color (variously #FFA400, #FFBF00, #F8B500) between orange and yellow ''yamabuki'' color ({{lang|ja|山吹色}} ''yamabuki-iro''), from the name of the plant. [[Qing Dynasty]] poet Chen Hao ({{lang|zh|陳淏}}) celebrated the beauty of ''Kerria japonica'' in his agricultural treatise the {{ill|Flower Mirror (book)|ja|花鏡 (陳コウ子)|zh|花镜|lt=''Flower Mirror''}} ({{lang|zh|花鏡}}). ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *{{Commons category-inline|Kerria japonica|''Kerria japonica''}} *{{Wikispecies-inline|Kerria (Rosaceae)|''Kerria''}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q157401|from2=Q3195486}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Kerrieae]] [[Category:Flora of Japan]] [[Category:Flora of China]] [[Category:Flora of Korea]] [[Category:Plants described in 1771]]
